label: A01
question: Can Weave show the screenshots that are already in our object storage without uploading another copy? Explain what we log and every required storage and team setup step.
answer:
Yes. You log only each screenshot's URI (its address in the bucket, such as `s3://...`) as a plain string. Weave then shows the image inline straight from your bucket. The image bytes stay in your bucket, and only the URI is sent to Weave [S1]. This is different from the Content API, which reads the bytes and stores a copy in Weave [S1].

**What you log**
- Put the URI as a string value anywhere in a trace, such as an Op's input or output. The field name doesn't matter, and you don't need a content annotation [S4, S6]. (An Op is a function you track with `@weave.op`.)
- Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`. The file extension decides how the file is shown: `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` images appear inline, and other formats appear as a download link [S4].

```python
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op
def record_step(screenshot_uri: str) -> dict:
    return {"screenshot": screenshot_uri}

record_step("s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/screens/step-001.png")
```
This follows the documented Op pattern [S6]. For an agent app, a separate agent-spans version of this guide exists [S6].

**Before you start**
- Your deployment must support the feature. It's available in Multi-tenant Cloud, and in preview for Dedicated Cloud and Self-Managed v0.84.0 or later [S5].
- You need a CoreWeave Forge account and API key, an S3 or GCS bucket you control with at least one object in it, and organization admin permissions [S5].

**Storage setup** (read-only access [S2])
- **AWS:** Add a bucket policy that gives `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration` the `s3:GetObject` permission. Then add a CORS rule (CORS lets the browser load files from another site) that allows `GET` and `HEAD` from `https://forge.coreweave.com`. If your objects use a customer-managed KMS key, that key's policy must also give the same role `kms:Decrypt` [S2].
- **GCS:** Give `wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com` the `roles/storage.objectViewer` role, and apply the same CORS rule [S2].

**Team setup**
1. Open `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings` and go to **Reference buckets** → **Add bucket** [S3].
2. Choose AWS or Google Cloud. Enter just the bucket name (no `s3://` or `gs://`) and the key of one existing object, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads that one object to confirm access and CORS work [S3].
3. Optionally select **Test connection**, then select **Add bucket** [S3].

URIs won't display as images until the bucket is registered [S3]. If Weave can't resolve a URI, for example because the object is missing, the trace shows the plain URI text instead [S7].

sources.heading: Configure your bucket
sources.text:
## Configure your bucket

Grant W\&B read access to the bucket and allow the browser to fetch objects with CORS.

When you view a trace, W\&B presigns a short-lived download URL for each referenced object. Grant the W\&B integration principal read access on the bucket so presigning can succeed. This is read-only access for inline rendering.

**AWS S3**

1. Apply a bucket policy that grants the W\&B integration principal `s3:GetObject`. Save the following as `bucket-policy.json`, replacing `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "Version": "2012-10-17",
     "Id": "WandBAccess",
     "Statement": [{
       "Sid": "WandbAccess",
       "Effect": "Allow",
       "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration"},
       "Action": "s3:GetObject",
       "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::[YOUR-BUCKET]/*"
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --policy file://bucket-policy.json
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "CORSRules": [{
       "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
       "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"],
       "AllowedOrigins": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
       "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"],
       "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-cors --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-configuration file://cors.json
   ```

> [!NOTE]
>
> If an object is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, its key policy must also grant `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration` `kms:Decrypt`. The bucket policy alone is not sufficient.

**Google Cloud Storage**

1. Grant the W\&B integration service account `roles/storage.objectViewer` on the bucket. Replace `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] \
     --member="serviceAccount:wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
     --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   [{
     "origin": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
     "method": ["GET", "HEAD"],
     "responseHeader": ["ETag"],
     "maxAgeSeconds": 3000
   }]
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets update gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-file=cors.json
   ```

At this point, Weight & Biases can read objects from your bucket, and the UI can fetch them in the browser.

## Register the reference bucket

Register the bucket in your team settings so Weave can presign and display referenced URIs.

1. Go to your team settings page (`https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`).
2. In the **Reference buckets** section, select **Add bucket**.
3. Select your cloud provider (**AWS** or **Google Cloud**).
4. For the bucket name, enter `[YOUR-BUCKET]` only — without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix.
5. For the object key, enter the key of an existing object in the bucket, for example `photos/cat.png` (the object key only, not a full URL). W\&B reads this one object to confirm it has read access and that CORS is configured correctly. This checks access only; once verified, presigning works for any object in the bucket.
6. Optionally, select **Test connection** to validate the configuration without saving.
7. Select **Add bucket** to save.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

label: A02
question: Our nightly test must keep using the wording we published last Friday even when teammates publish edits under the same prompt name. How can we retrieve that particular revision reliably?
answer:
Load the prompt by its exact version (preferably the version hash) instead of by name alone. Each `weave.publish` creates a new version that can't be changed afterward. A bare name always gives you `:latest`, which moves to whatever a teammate publishes next [S2, S1].

**Steps**

1. **Find Friday's version.** In the Weave project sidebar, open **Assets**, then **Prompts**, and click **(x) Versions** next to your prompt. If you need to confirm which version has the wording you published, select two versions and click **Compare** to see the differences [S6].
2. **Pin it in the test.** Use `name:<version>`, where `<version>` is the version hash or a version index such as `v3`. You can also use the full ref URI, a complete address that includes your team, project, prompt name and version [S1, S3]:
   `weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<prompt_name>:<version>`
3. **Load it with `.get()`.** A ref is a pointer to a stored version, and `.get()` fetches that version [S1].

```python
import weave

# Option A: short ref (requires weave.init)
weave.init("<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>")
prompt = weave.ref("<prompt_name>:<version_hash>").get()

# Option B: full ref URI (does not require weave.init)
prompt = weave.ref(
    "weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<prompt_name>:<version_hash>"
).get()
```

**Which to choose**
- **Version hash or index:** Points to one version, and that version can't be edited, so new publishes won't change what your test loads [S2, S3]. My suggestion, which the docs don't state directly, is the hash: it identifies the exact content you published.
- **Aliases (named labels such as `production`):** The docs recommend these for production because you can move them to a newer version and every consumer picks up the change [S4]. That's the wrong behavior for a test that must never change, unless you're the only one who moves the alias.

sources.heading: Retrieve a prompt version in code
sources.text:
## Retrieve a prompt version in code

To retrieve a prompt, create a reference to its name and version, then call `.get()` to load it. A ref points to a stored object; `.get()` fetches that object so you can use it in your application.

You can construct refs with a few different styles:

* `weave.ref(<name>)`: Retrieves the `:latest` version of a prompt. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>)`: Retrieves a prompt by alias, version hash, or version index. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>)`: Retrieves the prompt located at the specified [fully qualified ref URI](#construct-a-fully-qualified-ref-uri). Does not require calling `weave.init(...)`.

The following example loads the `support_prompt:v3` version so you can use it in your application:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

prompt = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()
```

sources.text:
## Construct a fully qualified ref URI

Before retrieving a prompt version in code, it helps to understand how Weave identifies stored objects. A fully qualified ref URI uniquely identifies a Weave object.

A fully qualified Weave object ref URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<object_name>:<object_version>
```

* `your-team-name`: Weights & Biases entity (username or team name)
* `your-project-name`: Weights & Biases project
* `object_name`: object name
* `object_version`: either a version hash, a version index like `v0` or `v1`, or an alias like `:latest` or `:production`. All objects have the `:latest` alias.

For example, a fully qualified Weave prompt URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3
```

sources.text:
## Use prompts in production

When deploying prompts in production systems, use an [alias](#add-prompt-tags-and-aliases) like `production` rather than a version index or the latest version. In your production application, load the prompt with `weave.ref(<name>:<alias>).get()`.

Using an alias keeps production behavior stable and predictable. When you're ready to promote a new version, move the alias to that version. All consumers then automatically pick up the change.

A common workflow looks like this:

1. Develop and test a new prompt version.
2. Evaluate the new prompt against datasets or evaluation suites.
3. Move the `production` alias to the new version with `client.set_aliases(new_ref, "production")`.

This approach lets teams safely iterate on prompts without unexpectedly changing production behavior.

## View and compare prompt versions

The Weights & Biases UI lets you browse all versions of a prompt and view side-by-side diffs between them, which is useful for reviewing how a prompt has evolved.

To view versions of the prompt in the UI:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.

2. In the Weave project sidebar, click **Assets**. This opens the Assets page.

label: A03
question: For one op_name, how do I request a daily total cost and mean latency from POST /calls/stats? Explain granularity and the usage_metrics and call_metrics fields.
answer:
To get daily figures for one op, send `POST /calls/stats` with `granularity` set to `86400`, which is one day in seconds. Put the op name in `filter.op_names`. Ask for total cost under `usage_metrics` and average latency under `call_metrics` [S1, S2].

```python
import os
import requests

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",   # inclusive, UTC ISO 8601
    "end": "2026-03-08T00:00:00Z",     # exclusive; defaults to now if omitted
    "granularity": 86400,              # one-day buckets
    "filter": {"op_names": ["[YOUR-OP-NAME]"]},
    "usage_metrics": [{"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}],
    "call_metrics": [{"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg"]}],
}

response = requests.post(
    "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats",
    json=payload,
    auth=("api", os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")),
)
print(response.json())
```

[S1, S2]

**Fields explained**
- **Required fields:** You must send `project_id` and `start` [S1]. A single query can cover at most 31 days [S2].
- **`granularity`:** The size of each time bucket, in seconds. For example, `3600` gives hourly buckets. If you leave it out, the size is chosen based on your time range. It will be adjusted if it would create more than 10,000 buckets. The `timezone` field (default `UTC`) controls where bucket boundaries fall. The response tells you the bucket size actually used [S1].
- **`usage_metrics`:** Token and cost metrics. Options are `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, the cache token metrics, `input_cost`, `output_cost` and `total_cost`. Results come back in `usage_buckets`, grouped by timestamp and model [S1, S2]. So each day has one row per model, for example with `sum_total_cost` [S2]. To get a single daily total across models, add those rows up yourself (this is my inference from the grouping).
- **`call_metrics`:** Per-call metrics: `latency_ms`, `call_count` and `error_count`. Results come back in `call_buckets`, grouped by timestamp only, not by model. For example, you get `avg_latency_ms` per day [S1, S2].
- **Metric options:** Each metric object takes `metric`, `aggregations` (default `["sum"]`) and optional `percentiles`, such as `[50, 95, 99]` [S1]. The guide lists `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min` and `max` as aggregations [S2].

## Export Call metrics

When you need aggregate insights, such as cost or latency trends, rather than the underlying Call records, use the metrics endpoint described in this section.

You can also use the Weave Service API's [POST `/calls/stats` endpoint](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-stats) to retrieve metrics about your Calls without retrieving the Call data itself. You can retrieve information about your Calls, such as latency and cost, and aggregate them by sum, average, minimum, maximum, and count. For example, you can retrieve:

* Total token usage
* Average latency
* Maximum tokens used
* Total cost
* Minimum input tokens

The endpoint provides several filtering options so you can target Calls made within specified times, and by other properties, such as:

* Op name
* Trace ID
* Thread ID
* User ID

The following example demonstrates how to retrieve Calls generated from an Op named `web_app` over two days. Replace `[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]` with your team and project names:

```python Python lines {10-11,16-24} theme={"system"}
import requests
import json
import os

url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats"

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
# Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
    "granularity": 86400,
    "filter": {
        "trace_roots_only": True,
        "op_names": ["web_app"]
    },
# Specify metrics and their aggregate function
    "usage_metrics": [
        {"metric": "total_tokens", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}
    ],
    "call_metrics": [
        {"metric": "call_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "error_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg", "min", "max"], "percentiles": [50, 95, 99]}
    ]
}

API_KEY = os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=("api", API_KEY))

print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))
```

    trace_roots_only: true,

// Specify metrics and their aggregate function
  usage_metrics: [
    { metric: "total_tokens", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "total_cost", aggregations: ["sum"] },
  ],

question: I changed both my assistant's instructions and its model settings. How do I keep those app revisions identifiable in Weave and inspect which individual test answers improved or regressed?
answer:
Put the instructions and the model settings into one Weave `Model`, and run the same evaluation on the old and new versions. Then open both runs in the **Compare evaluations** view and use its **Dataset results** tab to check each test answer.

**1. Make each app revision identifiable**
- A Weave `Model` combines data, such as configuration, with the code that runs it. To create one, subclass `weave.Model`, give every attribute a type, and add a typed `predict` method decorated with `@weave.op()` [S3].
- Weave records the model's settings with the inputs and outputs every time you call `predict()` [S3].
- When you change the attributes or the code that defines the model, Weave records the change and creates a new version. You can then compare predictions across versions, for example after editing a prompt or trying a different model [S1].
- If you store the instructions and the model settings as attributes, a change to either one should create a new version. That's my inference from how versioning works, not a separate documented rule.

**2. Score both versions with the same evaluation**
An evaluation (a dataset plus scorers) works like this: `evaluation.evaluate(model)` passes each dataset row into `model.predict`, matching column names to argument names. It then runs all the scorers and saves the results in Weave [S7]. In a Python script, wrap the call in `asyncio.run`. In a notebook, use `await` instead [S5].

```python
import asyncio
import weave

class Assistant(weave.Model):
    system_prompt: str
    model_name: str
    temperature: float

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, question: str) -> dict:
        # Replace with your LLM call using self.system_prompt, self.model_name, self.temperature
        return {"generated_text": "<MODEL_OUTPUT>"}

# Replace with your own test cases; column names must match predict() arguments
examples = [
    {"question": "<TEST_QUESTION>", "expected": "<EXPECTED_ANSWER>"},
]

@weave.op
def match_score(expected: str, model_output: dict) -> dict:
    # Replace with your own scoring logic
    return {"match": expected == model_output["generated_text"]}

weave.init("<YOUR_PROJECT>")
evaluation = weave.Evaluation(name="assistant_eval", dataset=examples, scorers=[match_score])

old = Assistant(system_prompt="<OLD_INSTRUCTIONS>", model_name="<OLD_MODEL>", temperature=0.7)
new = Assistant(system_prompt="<NEW_INSTRUCTIONS>", model_name="<NEW_MODEL>", temperature=0.2)
for m in (old, new):
    print(asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(m)))
```

**3. See which answers improved or regressed**
1. In the project sidebar, select **Evals**. Tick both evaluations and select **Compare** [S4].
2. The leftmost evaluation is the baseline, meaning the one the others are compared against. To change it, open the evaluation's action menu and choose **Make baseline**. Pick your old version [S4, S6].
3. Open **Dataset results**. Each row is one test example, showing the input next to each run's output and scores. Select a row for a side-by-side view [S2].
4. With exactly two evaluations, scatter plots show where examples diverge. Drag over a group of points to filter the table to those examples, and use the **Dimension** menu to choose the metric [S2].

This per-example table only appears if both runs share dataset rows, so evaluate both versions on the same dataset [S2].

## Automatic versioning of models

When you change the parameters or the code that defines your model, Weave logs these changes and updates the version.
This lets you compare predictions across versions of your model. Use this to iterate on prompts or to try a different LLM and compare predictions across settings.

For example, here you create a new model:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init('intro-example')

model = YourModel(attribute1='howdy', attribute2=10)
model.predict('world')
```

After calling this, you see that you now have two versions of this model in the UI, each with different tracked calls.

# Track application versions with models

> Track versions of your application with structured models that combine data and code.

A `Model` is a combination of data (which can include configuration, trained model weights, or other information) and code that defines how the model operates. By structuring your code to be compatible with this API, you benefit from a structured way to version your application so you can more systematically keep track of your experiments.

This guide shows you how to define a Weave `Model`, call it to capture inputs and outputs, take advantage of automatic versioning when your code or parameters change, serve the model behind a local API, and tag production calls for filtering. It's for developers who build LLM-powered applications with Weave and want a repeatable way to track and compare iterations of their app.

**Python**

To create a model in Weave, you need the following:

* A class that inherits from `weave.Model`
* Type definitions on all parameters
* A typed `predict` function with `@weave.op()` decorator

```python lines theme={"system"}
from weave import Model
import weave

class YourModel(Model):
    attribute1: str
    attribute2: int

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, input_data: str) -> dict:
        # Model logic goes here
        prediction = self.attribute1 + ' ' + input_data
        return {'pred': prediction}
```

You can call the model as usual with:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init('intro-example')

model = YourModel(attribute1='hello', attribute2=5)
model.predict('world')
```

This tracks the model settings along with the inputs and outputs anytime you call `predict()`. You now have a versioned Weave `Model` that records every prediction it makes, which the following sections build on.

sources.text:
### Dataset results tab

Select **Dataset results** to compare individual dataset examples across the selected evaluations. Each row corresponds to one dataset example and shows the dataset input alongside each evaluation's output and scorer metrics, so you can inspect where a specific example diverges. Select a row to open a side-by-side detail view.

When you compare exactly two evaluations, the tab shows two scatter plots above the table. In each plot, a point represents a dataset example, positioned by its metric value in each of the two evaluations, so examples where the evaluations diverge stand out. Select (brush) a region of points to filter the examples shown in the table, and use the **Dimension** menu on each plot to choose which metric it plots.

The Dataset results tab requires that the compared evaluations share dataset rows. If their datasets have no rows in common, no results table is displayed.

# Track application versions with models

> Track versions of your application with structured models that combine data and code.

A `Model` is a combination of data (which can include configuration, trained model weights, or other information) and code that defines how the model operates. By structuring your code to be compatible with this API, you benefit from a structured way to version your application so you can more systematically keep track of your experiments.

This guide shows you how to define a Weave `Model`, call it to capture inputs and outputs, take advantage of automatic versioning when your code or parameters change, serve the model behind a local API, and tag production calls for filtering. It's for developers who build LLM-powered applications with Weave and want a repeatable way to track and compare iterations of their app.

**Python**

To create a model in Weave, you need the following:

* A class that inherits from `weave.Model`
* Type definitions on all parameters
* A typed `predict` function with `@weave.op()` decorator

```python lines theme={"system"}
from weave import Model
import weave

class YourModel(Model):
    attribute1: str
    attribute2: int

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, input_data: str) -> dict:
        # Model logic goes here
        prediction = self.attribute1 + ' ' + input_data
        return {'pred': prediction}
```

You can call the model as usual with:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init('intro-example')

model = YourModel(attribute1='hello', attribute2=5)
model.predict('world')
```

This tracks the model settings along with the inputs and outputs anytime you call `predict()`. You now have a versioned Weave `Model` that records every prediction it makes, which the following sections build on.

## <kbd>class</kbd> `Evaluation`

Sets up an evaluation which includes a set of scorers and a dataset.

Calling evaluation.evaluate(model) will pass in rows from a dataset into a model matching  the names of the columns of the dataset to the argument names in model.predict.

Then it will call all of the scorers and save the results in weave.

If you want to preprocess the rows from the dataset you can pass in a function to preprocess\_model\_input.

**Examples:**

```python theme={"system"}
# Collect your examples
examples = [
     {"question": "What is the capital of France?", "expected": "Paris"},
     {"question": "Who wrote 'To Kill a Mockingbird'?", "expected": "Harper Lee"},
     {"question": "What is the square root of 64?", "expected": "8"},
]

# Define any custom scoring function
@weave.op
def match_score1(expected: str, model_output: dict) -> dict:
     # Here is where you'd define the logic to score the model output
     return {'match': expected == model_output['generated_text']}

@weave.op
def function_to_evaluate(question: str):
     # here's where you would add your LLM call and return the output
     return  {'generated_text': 'Paris'}

# Score your examples using scoring functions
evaluation = Evaluation(
     dataset=examples, scorers=[match_score1]
)

# Start tracking the evaluation
weave.init('intro-example')
# Run the evaluation
asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(function_to_evaluate))
```

* `name`: `str | None`
* `description`: `str | None`
* `ref`: `trace.refs.ObjectRef | None`
* `dataset`: `<class 'dataset.dataset.Dataset'>`

question: The pictures are already in S3, bucket permissions and CORS are set, and I trace both regular Python functions and an agent's tools. What setup remains, and what should each path record to display those pictures in Weave?
answer:
The main step left is to **register the bucket as a reference bucket for your Weave team**. After that, both paths record the same kind of value: the picture's `s3://` URI as a plain string. Weave doesn't upload the image. It stores only the URI, and the image stays in your bucket [S1].

**Remaining setup**
- Check the basics: you need a Forge account and API key, and an organization admin has to add the bucket. Adding a reference bucket needs the same permission as creating a team. The feature works in Multi-tenant Cloud. It's in preview for Dedicated Cloud and for Self-Managed v0.84.0 and later [S3].
- Go to `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`, find **Reference buckets**, and select **Add bucket**. Choose **AWS** and enter the bucket name without `s3://`. Then enter the key of one object that already exists, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads that one object to check read access and CORS (the browser-access rules you already set up). Once the check passes, Weave can create links for any object in the bucket. You can select **Test connection** first, then select **Add bucket** [S4].
- Until you register the bucket, the URIs show up only as text [S4]. Weave only turns `s3://` and `gs://` URIs into images when they point to a registered bucket [S2].

**What each path should record**
- **Regular Python functions (Weave ops):** pass the URI as an input or return it as an output, for example `"s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png"`. The field name doesn't matter [S2].
- **Agent tools:** inside a `weave.start_tool(...)` block, set `tool.result` to the URI string. That block goes inside `weave.start_conversation` and `weave.start_turn`. The picture then appears in the **Agents** view, on the tool call that returned it [S5, S6].

**How the pictures appear**
- When you open a trace, Weave swaps each URI for a short-lived presigned link (a temporary access link) and shows the image inline [S2].
- The file extension decides how it displays. Common formats like `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` show inline, and other formats show as a download link [S2].
- If the object is missing or the bucket isn't registered, you'll see the plain URI instead [S6].

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using agent spans

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in the Weave Agents view by returning their URIs from agent tool spans, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

question: I am adding postprocess_inputs and postprocess_output to a Python @weave.op. What types go into and out of each hook, and which representation is saved in the trace?
answer:
`postprocess_inputs` takes a dict of the call's arguments and returns a dict. `postprocess_output` takes whatever your function returns and returns a changed version of that value. The trace saves the changed versions, not the raw ones.

**`postprocess_inputs`**
- **Receives:** a dict mapping each argument name to its value (`dict[str, Any]`) [S1].
- **Returns:** a dict of the changed inputs, for example with a sensitive argument removed [S1].

**`postprocess_output`**
- **Receives:** whatever your function would normally return. The docs example uses a dataclass called `CustomObject` [S1].
- **Returns:** the changed output. The example returns a new `CustomObject` with `secret_password="REDACTED"`, so the type stays the same [S1].

**What the trace saves**
- Both hooks change the inputs and output "before logging" [S2]. They let you change what Weave logs without editing the original function, for example to hide sensitive data [S1]. So the trace stores what the hooks return.
- My reading (the docs don't say this outright): because the hooks only affect logging, your function still receives the original arguments, and callers still get the original return value.
- If you also pass `postprocess_inputs` / `postprocess_output` to `weave.init`, those apply to every op that client traces. They run after each op's own hooks, so the saved trace reflects both steps in that order [S3].

```python
from typing import Any
import weave

def postprocess_inputs(inputs: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {k: v for k, v in inputs.items() if k != "hide_me"}

def postprocess_output(output: Any) -> Any:
    return "REDACTED"  # replace with your own transformation

@weave.op(postprocess_inputs=postprocess_inputs, postprocess_output=postprocess_output)
def func(a: int, hide_me: str) -> str:
    return hide_me

weave.init("your-project-name")
func(a=1, hide_me="password123")
```

This feature is Python-only for now. It isn't available in TypeScript yet [S1].

### <kbd>function</kbd> `setup_dunder_weave_dict`

```python theme={"system"}
setup_dunder_weave_dict(op: 'Op', d: 'WeaveKwargs | None' = None) → WeaveKwargs
```

Sets up a \_\_weave dict used to pass WeaveKwargs to ops.

* **`func`**: The function to decorate.
* **`name`**: Custom name for the op. Defaults to the function name.
* **`call_display_name`**: Display name for calls, can be a string or callable.
* **`postprocess_inputs`**: Function to transform inputs before logging.
* **`postprocess_output`**: Function to transform output before logging.
* **`tracing_sample_rate`**: Fraction of calls to trace (0.0 to 1.0).
* **`enable_code_capture`**: Whether to capture source code for this op.
* **`accumulator`**: Function to accumulate results for streaming ops.
* **`attributes`**: Default attributes merged into every call this op creates,  at the lowest precedence. A `weave.attributes()` context and explicit  per-call attributes override them on key collision. The reserved  "weave" key may not be set here.
* **`eager_call_start`**: If True, call starts are sent immediately rather than batched.  Useful for long-running operations like evaluations that should  be visible in the UI immediately.

**Args:**

* **`d`**: Optional existing WeaveKwargs dict to update.
* **`op`**: Op to extract kind and color from.

### <kbd>function</kbd> `init`

```python theme={"system"}
init(
    project_name: 'str',
    settings: 'UserSettings | dict[str, Any] | None' = None,
    autopatch_settings: 'AutopatchSettings | None' = None,
    postprocess_inputs: 'PostprocessInputsFunc | None' = None,
    postprocess_output: 'PostprocessOutputFunc | None' = None,
    attributes: 'dict[str, Any] | None' = None,
    global_postprocess_inputs: 'PostprocessInputsFunc | None' = None,
    global_postprocess_output: 'PostprocessOutputFunc | None' = None,
    global_attributes: 'dict[str, Any] | None' = None
) → WeaveClient
```

Initialize weave tracking, logging to a wandb project.

Logging is initialized globally, so you do not need to keep a reference to the return value of init.

Following init, calls of weave.op decorated functions will be logged to the specified project.

**Args:**

NOTE: Client-level postprocessing runs after each op's own postprocessing. The order is always: 1. Op-specific postprocessing 2. Client-level postprocessing

* **`project_name`**: The name of the Weights & Biases team and project to log to. If you don't  specify a team, your default entity is used. To find or update your default entity, refer to [User settings](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/app/settings-page/user-settings.md#default-team) in the W\&B documentation.
* **`settings`**: Configuration for the Weave client generally. Can be a UserSettings instance or a dict  with any of the following keys (all optional). All settings can also be configured  via environment variables using the prefix WEAVE\_ (e.g., WEAVE\_DISABLED=true).  Available settings: - `disabled` (bool): Disables traces on all functions. Default: `False` - `print_call_link` (bool): Prints links in terminal to Weave UI for ops. Default: `True` - `log_level` (str): Sets what type of information to log (`DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `CRITICAL`). Default: `INFO` - `display_viewer` (str): Controls how Weave displays objects in the console (`auto`, `rich`, `print`). Default: `auto` - `capture_code` (bool): Captures code of traced ops to your Weave project. Default: `True` - `implicitly_patch_integrations` (bool): Auto-patches supported libraries. Default: `True` - `redact_pii` (bool): Scans all trace data for sensitive information,  like emails, phone numbers, and credit cards, and replaces them with placeholder values  before sending to the server. Requires presidio-analyzer and presidio-anonymizer packages.
* **`Default`**: `False` - `redact_pii_fields` (list\[str]): Specifies which PII entity types to redact when `redact_pii` is True. If empty, uses Presidio's default set. Examples  \['EMAIL','PHONE\_NUMBER','CREDIT\_CARD','US\_SSN']. See full list at  [https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/supported\_entities/](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/supported_entities/)
* **`Default`**: `[]` - `redact_pii_exclude_fields` (list\[str]): PII entity types to exclude. Default: `[]` - `capture_client_info` (bool): Captures Python/SDK version info. Default: `True` - `capture_system_info` (bool): Captures OS information. Default: `True` - `client_parallelism` (int): Number of workers for background ops. Default: `auto` - `use_server_cache` (bool): Enables local disk caching of server responses. - `server_cache_size_limit` (int): Cache size limit in bytes. Default: `1_000_000_000` - `server_cache_dir` (str): Directory for server cache. Default: `temporary` - `scorers_dir` (str): Directory for scorer model checkpoints. Default: `~/.cache/wandb/weave-scorers` - `max_calls_queue_size` (int): Maximum queue size (0 = unbounded). Default: `100_000` - `retry_max_interval` (float): Maximum retry interval in seconds. Default: `300` - `retry_max_attempts` (int): Maximum number of retries. Default: `3` - `enable_disk_fallback` (bool): Writes dropped items to disk. Default: `True` - `use_parallel_table_upload` (bool): Enables parallel chunked upload for large tables. If False, tables are uploaded sequentially in smaller chunks.
* **`Default`**: `True` - `http_timeout` (float): Maximum time in seconds to wait for HTTP requests to complete. This includes connection time, data transfer, and server processing. Increase for slow networks or when working with large payloads.
* **`Default`**: `30.0` - `use_stainless_server` (bool): Uses the Stainless-generated HTTP client which provides better type safety, automatic retries, and improved error handling. This is experimental and may become the default in future versions.
* **`Default`**: `False` - `use_calls_complete` (bool): Uses an optimized write path that batches complete call data (start and end) into a single request instead of separate start/end requests. This reduces server load and improves performance, especially for short-lived ops.
* **`Default`**: `True` - `use_otel_v2`: (bool): Routes OTel-capable integrations through their OTel variant.
* **`Default`**: `True`
* **`autopatch_settings`**: (Deprecated) Configuration for autopatch integrations. Use explicit patching instead.
* **`postprocess_inputs`**: A function applied to the inputs of every op traced by this client.
* **`postprocess_output`**: A function applied to the output of every op traced by this client.
* **`attributes`**: A dictionary of attributes applied to every trace produced by this client.

**Returns:**
A Weave client.

label: A07
question: Our nightly test must keep using the wording we published last Friday even when teammates publish edits under the same prompt name. How can we retrieve that particular revision reliably?
answer:
Pin the test to Friday's exact version (its version hash or version index), not to the bare prompt name, `:latest`, or an alias. Each `weave.publish` creates a new version that can't be changed afterwards, and earlier versions are kept. So when teammates publish edits under the same name, Friday's wording stays available [S2, S6].

**Steps**

1. **Find Friday's version.** In the project, go to **Assets** → **Prompts**, then click **(x) Versions** for your prompt. To confirm you have the right wording, tick two versions and click **Compare** to see the differences [S7].
2. **Note its version ID.** A version can be identified by its version hash, by its index (such as `v3`), or by an alias (such as `:latest` or `:production`) [S4].
3. **Load that version in the test.** A ref (reference) points to a stored version, and `.get()` loads it [S1]:

```python
import weave

weave.init("<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>")
prompt = weave.ref("<prompt_name>:<version_hash_or_index>").get()
```

You can skip `weave.init` by using the fully qualified ref instead [S1, S4]:

```python
import weave

prompt = weave.ref(
    "weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<prompt_name>:<version_hash_or_index>"
).get()
```

**What to avoid**
- `weave.ref("<prompt_name>")` always loads `:latest`, so it will pick up teammates' edits [S1].
- Aliases can be moved to a different version, and everything using that alias then switches automatically [S5]. That's useful for production, but not if the test must stay frozen on Friday's wording.

My inference: either the hash or the index will keep pointing to Friday's version because versions can't be changed after publishing. The hash is the safer choice if you want to avoid any doubt about which number belongs to which version.

sources.heading: Retrieve a prompt version in code
sources.text:
## Retrieve a prompt version in code

To retrieve a prompt, create a reference to its name and version, then call `.get()` to load it. A ref points to a stored object; `.get()` fetches that object so you can use it in your application.

You can construct refs with a few different styles:

* `weave.ref(<name>)`: Retrieves the `:latest` version of a prompt. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>)`: Retrieves a prompt by alias, version hash, or version index. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>)`: Retrieves the prompt located at the specified [fully qualified ref URI](#construct-a-fully-qualified-ref-uri). Does not require calling `weave.init(...)`.

The following example loads the `support_prompt:v3` version so you can use it in your application:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

prompt = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()
```

sources.heading: Construct a fully qualified ref URI
sources.text:
## Construct a fully qualified ref URI

Before retrieving a prompt version in code, it helps to understand how Weave identifies stored objects. A fully qualified ref URI uniquely identifies a Weave object.

A fully qualified Weave object ref URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<object_name>:<object_version>
```

* `your-team-name`: Weights & Biases entity (username or team name)
* `your-project-name`: Weights & Biases project
* `object_name`: object name
* `object_version`: either a version hash, a version index like `v0` or `v1`, or an alias like `:latest` or `:production`. All objects have the `:latest` alias.

For example, a fully qualified Weave prompt URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3
```

sources.heading: Use prompts in production
sources.text:
## Use prompts in production

When deploying prompts in production systems, use an [alias](#add-prompt-tags-and-aliases) like `production` rather than a version index or the latest version. In your production application, load the prompt with `weave.ref(<name>:<alias>).get()`.

Using an alias keeps production behavior stable and predictable. When you're ready to promote a new version, move the alias to that version. All consumers then automatically pick up the change.

A common workflow looks like this:

1. Develop and test a new prompt version.
2. Evaluate the new prompt against datasets or evaluation suites.
3. Move the `production` alias to the new version with `client.set_aliases(new_ref, "production")`.

This approach lets teams safely iterate on prompts without unexpectedly changing production behavior.

sources.heading: How prompt versions are created
sources.text:
## How prompt versions are created

Weave automatically tracks every version of your prompts, creating a complete history of how your prompts evolve. This versioning system is important for prompt engineering workflows. It lets you experiment safely, track what changes improved or hurt performance, and roll back to previous versions if needed. Each time you publish a prompt with the same name but different content, Weave creates a new version while preserving all previous versions.

Each version is immutable. Once created, the contents of that version cannot be changed. If you update a prompt and publish it again, Weave creates a new version while preserving previous versions.

Versioning enables you to:

* Reproduce past experiments.
* Safely iterate on prompt changes.
* Roll out prompt updates in a controlled way.

label: A08
question: Can Weave show the screenshots that are already in our object storage without uploading another copy? Explain what we log and every required storage and team setup step.
answer:
Yes. Weave can show screenshots that are already in your S3 or Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket without uploading them again. You log each screenshot's bucket address (its URI, such as `s3://...`) as a plain string. Weave then displays the image from your bucket, and the image bytes stay there [S1]. This is a different method from the Content API, which reads the bytes and stores a copy in Weave [S1].

**What you log**
- Log the URI as a string anywhere in a trace: an Op's input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name doesn't matter [S4]. An Op is a function you track with `@weave.op`.
- Only `s3://` and `gs://` URIs are supported. Weave only resolves URIs in buckets registered for your team [S4].
- The file extension decides how it shows up. `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` display inline, while unrecognised formats appear as download links [S4].

```python
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op
def record_step(screenshot_uri: str) -> dict:
    return {"screenshot": screenshot_uri}

record_step("s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/screens/step1.png")
```
This follows the documented pattern [S6]. If you trace an agent app, the docs have a separate page on doing this with agent spans [S6].

**Before you start**
- Your deployment must support it. It's generally available on Multi-tenant Cloud, and in preview on Dedicated Cloud and Self-Managed v0.84.0 or later [S5].
- You need a CoreWeave Forge account and API key, a bucket containing at least one object, and organisation admin permission [S5].

**Bucket setup**
When someone views a trace, W&B creates a short-lived download link (a presigned URL) for each object. It needs read access to do this [S2].
- **S3:** Add a bucket policy that grants `s3:GetObject` to `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration`. Then add a CORS rule allowing `GET` and `HEAD` from `https://forge.coreweave.com` [S2]. CORS is the browser setting that lets the Weave web app load files from your bucket. If you encrypt objects with a customer-managed KMS key, the key policy must also grant that role `kms:Decrypt` [S2].
- **GCS:** Grant `roles/storage.objectViewer` to `wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and add the same CORS rule [S2].

**Team setup**
1. Open `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings` and go to **Reference buckets** → **Add bucket** [S3].
2. Choose AWS or Google Cloud. Enter the bucket name without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix [S3].
3. Enter the key of one existing object, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads it once to check read access and CORS [S3].
4. You can select **Test connection** first if you like. Then select **Add bucket** [S3].

Screenshot URIs won't display until the bucket is registered [S3].

sources.text:
# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

sources.heading: Configure your bucket
sources.text:
## Configure your bucket

Grant W\&B read access to the bucket and allow the browser to fetch objects with CORS.

When you view a trace, W\&B presigns a short-lived download URL for each referenced object. Grant the W\&B integration principal read access on the bucket so presigning can succeed. This is read-only access for inline rendering.

**AWS S3**

1. Apply a bucket policy that grants the W\&B integration principal `s3:GetObject`. Save the following as `bucket-policy.json`, replacing `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "Version": "2012-10-17",
     "Id": "WandBAccess",
     "Statement": [{
       "Sid": "WandbAccess",
       "Effect": "Allow",

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: Register the reference bucket
sources.text:
## Register the reference bucket

Register the bucket in your team settings so Weave can presign and display referenced URIs.

1. Go to your team settings page (`https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`).
2. In the **Reference buckets** section, select **Add bucket**.
3. Select your cloud provider (**AWS** or **Google Cloud**).
4. For the bucket name, enter `[YOUR-BUCKET]` only — without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix.
5. For the object key, enter the key of an existing object in the bucket, for example `photos/cat.png` (the object key only, not a full URL). W\&B reads this one object to confirm it has read access and that CORS is configured correctly. This checks access only; once verified, presigning works for any object in the bucket.
6. Optionally, select **Test connection** to validate the configuration without saving.
7. Select **Add bucket** to save.

label: A09
question: The pictures are already in S3, bucket permissions and CORS are set, and I trace both regular Python functions and an agent's tools. What setup remains, and what should each path record to display those pictures in Weave?
answer:
The one step left is to **register the bucket as a reference bucket** in your Weave team settings. After that, both paths only need to record the S3 URI as a plain string. Weave doesn't upload the image itself. It sends only the URI and shows the picture straight from your bucket [S1].

**Remaining setup**
- Requirements: Organization admin permissions, because adding a reference bucket needs the same permission as creating a team. This works on W&B Multi-tenant Cloud. It's in preview on Dedicated Cloud and on Self-Managed v0.84.0+ [S5].
- Go to `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings` → **Reference buckets** → **Add bucket**. Choose **AWS** and enter the bucket name without `s3://`. Then enter the key of one existing object, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads that object to confirm it has read access and that CORS works. You can select **Test connection** first, then **Add bucket** to save [S2].
- Until you register the bucket, the URIs won't show as images [S2]. Weave only resolves `s3://` or `gs://` URIs in buckets registered for your team [S1].

**What each path should record**
- **Regular functions (`@weave.op`)**: Put the URI as a string in an input or output, for example `return {"image": "s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/photos/cat.png", "caption": caption}`. The field name doesn't matter, and you don't need any content annotation [S4].
- **Agent tools (agent spans)**: Inside `weave.start_conversation(...)` → `weave.start_turn(...)` → `weave.start_tool(...)`, set the URI as the tool result: `tool.result = "s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png"`. The picture appears in the **Agents** view, on the tool call that returned it [S3].

**Both paths:** The file extension controls how it displays. `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` show as images, and unsupported formats show as a download link [S1].

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

label: A10
question: For one op_name, how do I request a daily total cost and mean latency from POST /calls/stats? Explain granularity and the usage_metrics and call_metrics fields.
answer:
To get daily stats for one op, send `POST https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats` with these settings:

- `granularity: 86400`, which is one day in seconds.
- `filter.op_names` set to your one op.
- A `usage_metrics` entry for `total_cost` with `sum`.
- A `call_metrics` entry for `latency_ms` with `avg`.

[S1, S2]

```python
import os
import requests

url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats"
payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",      # inclusive start time (UTC)
    "end": "2026-03-08T00:00:00Z",        # exclusive end time; leave out to mean "now"
    "granularity": 86400,                 # one-day buckets
    "timezone": "UTC",                    # where day boundaries fall
    "filter": {"op_names": ["[YOUR-OP-NAME]"]},
    "usage_metrics": [{"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}],
    "call_metrics": [{"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg"]}],
}
response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=("api", os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")))
print(response.json())
```

Only `project_id` and `start` are required. The time range can be at most 31 days. [S1, S2] The docs' own example also adds `"trace_roots_only": True` to the filter, which limits results to top-level (root) calls. [S1]

**Granularity**
- This is the width of each time "bucket", in seconds. If you leave it out, the server picks a size based on your time range. It will also change your value if it would create more than 10,000 buckets. [S2]
- `timezone` sets how buckets line up, for example `America/New_York`. The default is UTC. The response shows the bucket size actually used. [S2]

**`usage_metrics`**
- Covers token and cost metrics, such as `input_tokens`, `total_tokens`, `input_cost`, `output_cost` and `total_cost`. Results are grouped by time and by model. [S2]
- Results come back in `usage_buckets`, with one row per day per model, holding values like `sum_total_cost`. [S1, S2]
- **What this means for you:** if your op used more than one model, add up that day's rows to get the daily total. That adding-up step is my own inference; the docs don't state it.

**`call_metrics`**
- Covers `latency_ms`, `call_count` and `error_count`. Results are grouped by time only, not by model. [S2]
- Results come back in `call_buckets`, with one row per day holding `avg_latency_ms`. [S1]

**Both fields**
- Each entry takes `metric`, `aggregations` (defaults to `["sum"]`) and optional `percentiles`, such as `[50, 95]`. [S2]

## Export Call metrics

When you need aggregate insights, such as cost or latency trends, rather than the underlying Call records, use the metrics endpoint described in this section.

You can also use the Weave Service API's [POST `/calls/stats` endpoint](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-stats) to retrieve metrics about your Calls without retrieving the Call data itself. You can retrieve information about your Calls, such as latency and cost, and aggregate them by sum, average, minimum, maximum, and count. For example, you can retrieve:

* Total token usage
* Average latency
* Maximum tokens used
* Total cost
* Minimum input tokens

The endpoint provides several filtering options so you can target Calls made within specified times, and by other properties, such as:

* Op name
* Trace ID
* Thread ID
* User ID

The following example demonstrates how to retrieve Calls generated from an Op named `web_app` over two days. Replace `[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]` with your team and project names:

```python Python lines {10-11,16-24} theme={"system"}
import requests
import json
import os

url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats"

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
# Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
    "granularity": 86400,
    "filter": {
        "trace_roots_only": True,
        "op_names": ["web_app"]
    },
# Specify metrics and their aggregate function
    "usage_metrics": [
        {"metric": "total_tokens", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}
    ],
    "call_metrics": [
        {"metric": "call_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "error_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg", "min", "max"], "percentiles": [50, 95, 99]}
    ]
}

API_KEY = os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=("api", API_KEY))

print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))
```

```typescript TypeScript lines {6-7,13-20} theme={"system"}
const url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats";

const payload = {
  project_id: "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
  start: "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
// Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
  granularity: 86400,
  filter: {
    trace_roots_only: true,
    op_names: ["web_app"],
  },
// Specify metrics and their aggregate function
  usage_metrics: [
    { metric: "total_tokens", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "total_cost", aggregations: ["sum"] },
  ],
  call_metrics: [
    { metric: "call_count", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "error_count", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "latency_ms", aggregations: ["avg", "min", "max"], percentiles: [50, 95, 99] },
  ],
};

const API_KEY = [REDACTED_SECRET];

const response = await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    Authorization: "[REDACTED_SECRET]" + btoa(`api:${API_KEY}`),
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
});

const data = await response.json();
console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));
```

The request also specifies how to aggregate the metrics. You can aggregate metrics by `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, and `count`.

The endpoint returns a JSON object. The following example response shows two days' worth of metrics. Each day (bucket) appears as its own object in the `usage_buckets` and `call_buckets` arrays. Each array breaks down the metrics differently:

* `usage_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day by the model used.
* `call_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day regardless of the model used.

Set the granularity field (in seconds) in the request to change the bucket size.

question: I changed both my assistant's instructions and its model settings. How do I keep those app revisions identifiable in Weave and inspect which individual test answers improved or regressed?
answer:
Put the assistant's instructions and model settings into a `weave.Model`. Then run the same `Evaluation` (a fixed set of test examples plus scoring functions) on each version, and compare the runs in the **Compare evaluations** view.

**1. Keep each version identifiable**
- A Weave `Model` combines settings (data) with the code that uses them. To create one, write a class that inherits from `weave.Model`, give every parameter a type, and add a typed `predict` method decorated with `@weave.op()`. Weave then records the model's settings, inputs and outputs each time you call `predict()` [S3].
- When you change the model's parameters or code, Weave logs the change and creates a new version. You can then compare predictions across versions, which suits prompt changes and LLM swaps [S1].

```python
import asyncio
import weave

class Assistant(weave.Model):
    system_prompt: str
    model_name: str
    temperature: float

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, question: str) -> dict:
        # Call your LLM here using self.system_prompt, self.model_name, self.temperature
        return {"generated_text": "<MODEL_OUTPUT>"}

weave.init("<YOUR_PROJECT>")
evaluation = weave.Evaluation(dataset=examples, scorers=[my_scorer])  # placeholders

v1 = Assistant(system_prompt="<OLD_INSTRUCTIONS>", model_name="<OLD_MODEL>", temperature=0.2)
v2 = Assistant(system_prompt="<NEW_INSTRUCTIONS>", model_name="<NEW_MODEL>", temperature=0.7)
asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(v1))
asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(v2))
```
Each `.evaluate()` call runs `predict` on every example and scores each output with every scoring function [S6].

**2. See which test answers improved or regressed**
1. In the project sidebar, select **Evals**. Tick the checkbox for both runs, then select **Compare**. The leftmost run is the baseline, and every other run is compared against it [S5]. To use a different run as the reference, choose **Make baseline** from that run's action menu [S7].
2. Open the **Dataset results** tab [S2]. Each row is one test example, showing its input next to each run's output and scores. Select a row to see the outputs side by side [S4].
3. When you compare exactly two runs, the tab also shows scatter plots. Each point is one example, so examples whose scores differ between the runs stand out. Drag across a region of points to filter the table to those examples, and use the **Dimension** menu to choose which score each plot shows [S4].

**Requirement:** both runs must use at least some of the same dataset rows. If they share no rows, the per-example table doesn't appear [S4]. Reusing one `Evaluation` dataset for both versions avoids this.

## Automatic versioning of models

When you change the parameters or the code that defines your model, Weave logs these changes and updates the version.
This lets you compare predictions across versions of your model. Use this to iterate on prompts or to try a different LLM and compare predictions across settings.

For example, here you create a new model:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init('intro-example')

model = YourModel(attribute1='howdy', attribute2=10)
model.predict('world')
```

After calling this, you see that you now have two versions of this model in the UI, each with different tracked calls.

# Track application versions with models

> Track versions of your application with structured models that combine data and code.

A `Model` is a combination of data (which can include configuration, trained model weights, or other information) and code that defines how the model operates. By structuring your code to be compatible with this API, you benefit from a structured way to version your application so you can more systematically keep track of your experiments.

This guide shows you how to define a Weave `Model`, call it to capture inputs and outputs, take advantage of automatic versioning when your code or parameters change, serve the model behind a local API, and tag production calls for filtering. It's for developers who build LLM-powered applications with Weave and want a repeatable way to track and compare iterations of their app.

**Python**

To create a model in Weave, you need the following:

* A class that inherits from `weave.Model`
* Type definitions on all parameters
* A typed `predict` function with `@weave.op()` decorator

```python lines theme={"system"}
from weave import Model
import weave

class YourModel(Model):
    attribute1: str
    attribute2: int

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, input_data: str) -> dict:
        # Model logic goes here
        prediction = self.attribute1 + ' ' + input_data
        return {'pred': prediction}
```

You can call the model as usual with:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init('intro-example')

model = YourModel(attribute1='hello', attribute2=5)
model.predict('world')
```

This tracks the model settings along with the inputs and outputs anytime you call `predict()`. You now have a versioned Weave `Model` that records every prediction it makes, which the following sections build on.

### Dataset results tab

Select **Dataset results** to compare individual dataset examples across the selected evaluations. # PII Data Handling

> Handle personally identifiable information (PII) in LLM applications using W&B Weave's data redaction and filtering tools.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is an interactive notebook. You can run it locally or use the links below:
>
> * [Open in Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/pii.ipynb)
> * [View source on GitHub](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/pii.ipynb)

In this guide, you learn how to use W\&B Weave while ensuring your Personally Identifiable Information (PII) data remains private. Protecting PII helps you meet privacy and compliance requirements while still benefiting from LLM tracing and evaluation. This guide is intended for developers integrating Weave into LLM applications that process sensitive user data.

The guide demonstrates the following methods to identify, redact, and anonymize PII data:

1. **Regular expressions** to identify PII data and redact it.
2. **Microsoft's [Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/)**, a Python-based data protection SDK. This tool provides redaction and replacement functionality.
3. **[Faker](https://faker.readthedocs.io/en/master/)**, a Python library to generate fake data, combined with Presidio to anonymize PII data.

Additionally, you learn how to use *`weave.op` input/output logging customization* and *`autopatch_settings`* to integrate PII redaction and anonymization into the workflow. For more information, see [Customize logged inputs and outputs](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/ops.md#customize-logged-inputs-and-outputs).

To get started, do the following:

1. Review the [Overview](#overview) section.
2. Complete the [prerequisites](#prerequisites).
3. Review the [available methods](#redaction-methods-overview) for identifying, redacting, and anonymizing PII data.
4. [Apply the methods to Weave calls](#apply-the-methods-to-weave-calls).
